title: Production Function
description: Class 11 Economics: production, inputs and outputs, the production function, short run vs long run, total, average and marginal product, and the law of variable proportions.

topics.title: Production, the Production Function and Time Periods
topics.concept:
Production means creating goods and services to satisfy human wants — or, more precisely, creating utility by transforming inputs into output. The things used in production are the inputs (factors of production): land, labour, capital and enterprise. What comes out is the output.

The production function shows the technical relationship between inputs and output — the maximum output that can be produced from a given combination of inputs, with a given technology. In symbols, output Q depends on the factors used:

Q = f (L, K)

meaning the quantity of output Q is a function of labour (L) and capital (K) used. The production function only tells us the physical relation between inputs and output, not costs or prices.

Production is studied over two time periods:

  • Short run — a period in which at least one factor is fixed (usually capital, like the factory and machines) and only the other factors (like labour) can be varied. Output is changed only by changing the variable factor.
  • Long run — a period long enough for all factors to be varied; there are no fixed factors. The firm can change even its plant size.

The short run gives us the Law of Variable Proportions, and the long run gives us the laws of returns to scale. In Class 11 we focus mainly on the short-run behaviour of output.

examples.problem: Example 1: What does the production function show?
examples.solution:
It links inputs to output.

  • The technical relationship between inputs and output.
  • The maximum output from a given combination of inputs (with given technology).
examples.answer: The production function shows the technical relationship between inputs and the maximum output obtainable from them.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between the short run and the long run?
examples.solution:
It depends on which factors can vary.

  • Short run: at least one factor is fixed (only some factors vary).
  • Long run: all factors can be varied.
examples.answer: In the short run at least one factor is fixed; in the long run all factors can be varied.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the four factors of production.
examples.solution:
These are the inputs.

  • Land, labour, capital and enterprise (entrepreneur).

recap:
• Production = creating utility by turning inputs (land, labour, capital, enterprise) into output.
  • Production function: Q = f(L, K) — the technical input–output relation (physical, not cost).
  • Short run: at least one factor fixed; long run: all factors variable.

quiz.q: The production function shows the relationship between inputs and:
quiz.explanation: It is the technical relationship between inputs and output.

quiz.q: In the short run, at least one factor of production is:
quiz.explanation: The short run has at least one fixed factor.

topics.title: Total, Average and Marginal Product
topics.concept:
To study how output changes as we use more of a variable factor (say labour), we use three measures of product:

  • Total Product (TP) — the total quantity of output produced by all the units of the variable factor.
  • Average Product (AP) — output per unit of the variable factor: AP = TP ÷ L (where L is the units of the variable factor).
  • Marginal Product (MP) — the addition to total product when one more unit of the variable factor is used: MP = change in TP (TPₙ − TPₙ₋₁).

examples.problem: Example 1: Write the formulas for average product and marginal product.
examples.solution:
One is per unit, one is the addition.

  • AP = TP ÷ L (output per unit of variable factor).
  • MP = change in TP (TPₙ − TPₙ₋₁).
examples.answer: AP = TP ÷ L; MP = change in TP (TPₙ − TPₙ₋₁).

examples.problem: Example 2: From the table, what is the marginal product of the 4th unit of labour?

examples.solution:
Look at MP.

  • TP is maximum when MP = 0 (here at L = 6).
  • If MP becomes negative, TP falls.
examples.answer: TP is maximum when MP = 0; beyond that (MP negative) TP falls.

recap:
• TP = total output; AP = TP ÷ L; MP = change in TP.
  • TP rises while MP > 0, is maximum at MP = 0, falls if MP negative.
  • MP cuts AP at AP's maximum; MP > AP → AP rises, MP < AP → AP falls.

quiz.explanation: AP = total product ÷ units of the variable factor.

topics.title: The Law of Variable Proportions
topics.concept:
The behaviour of marginal product in the short run is summed up by the Law of Variable Proportions (also called the law of diminishing returns). It states: as we use more and more units of a variable factor with a fixed factor, the marginal product first rises, then falls, and finally becomes negative. This happens because the proportion between the fixed and variable factors keeps changing.

The law works in three stages (look back at the table):

  • Stage I — Increasing returns: TP rises at an increasing rate and MP rises. This happens because the fixed factor is under-used, and adding variable units improves efficiency (better division of labour).
  • Stage II — Diminishing returns: TP rises but at a decreasing rate; MP falls but is still positive (until TP is maximum). This is the most important stage — a rational producer always operates here, because output is still rising. The fixed factor is now being used closer to its best capacity.
  • Stage III — Negative returns: TP actually falls and MP becomes negative. There are now too many variable units crowding the fixed factor, so output drops. No sensible producer operates here.

Why do diminishing returns set in? Because the fixed factor (land, machinery) cannot be increased in the short run; as more variable units are added, each has less of the fixed factor to work with, so the extra output (MP) eventually falls. The Law of Variable Proportions is one of the most fundamental laws of production and explains why a firm cannot keep raising output indefinitely just by adding more workers to a fixed plant.

examples.problem: Example 1: State the Law of Variable Proportions.
examples.solution:
It describes how MP behaves.

  • As more units of a variable factor are used with a fixed factor, MP first rises, then falls, and finally becomes negative.
examples.answer: As more of a variable factor is combined with a fixed factor, marginal product first rises, then falls, and finally becomes negative.

examples.problem: Example 2: In which stage does a rational producer operate, and why?
examples.solution:
The sensible stage.

  • Stage II (diminishing returns).
  • Because TP is still rising (MP positive); Stage III has falling output and Stage I has the fixed factor under-used.
examples.answer: Stage II (diminishing returns), because total product is still rising there (MP positive) — Stage III gives falling output.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why do diminishing returns eventually set in?
examples.solution:
The fixed factor is limited.

  • The fixed factor cannot be increased in the short run.
  • As more variable units are added, each has less of the fixed factor, so MP falls.
examples.answer: Because the fixed factor cannot be increased in the short run, so each extra variable unit has less of it to work with and adds less output (MP falls).

recap:
• Law of Variable Proportions: with a fixed factor, MP of the variable factor first rises, then falls, then turns negative.
  • Stage I increasing returns (MP rises); Stage II diminishing returns (MP falls, positive) — rational stage; Stage III negative returns (TP falls, MP negative).
  • Cause: the fixed factor can't be increased in the short run.

quiz.q: In the Law of Variable Proportions, marginal product first rises, then falls, and finally becomes:
quiz.explanation: MP first rises, then falls, then turns negative (Stage III).
Stage II is the rational stage — output is still rising.

questions.q: Production means creating ____ to satisfy wants.
questions.explanation: Production creates utility by transforming inputs into output.

questions.q: Land, labour, capital and enterprise are the:
questions.explanation: These are the four factors of production (inputs).

questions.q: The technical relationship between inputs and output is the:
questions.explanation: It is the production function, Q = f(L, K).

questions.q: A period in which at least one factor is fixed is the:
questions.explanation: The short run has at least one fixed factor.

questions.q: In the long run, the number of fixed factors is:
questions.explanation: In the long run all factors can be varied — none are fixed.

questions.q: Total output produced by all units of the variable factor is:
questions.explanation: That total is the total product (TP).

questions.q: Average product equals:
questions.explanation: AP = total product ÷ units of the variable factor.

questions.q: Marginal product is the:
options: Addition to TP from one more unit
questions.explanation: MP is the change in TP from one more variable unit.

Total product is maximum when marginal product is:
questions.explanation: TP is maximum where MP = 0.

questions.q: The MP curve cuts the AP curve at AP's:
questions.explanation: MP intersects AP at the maximum point of AP.

questions.q: When MP is greater than AP, the AP is:
questions.explanation: AP rises while MP exceeds it.

questions.q: The law of variable proportions operates in the:
questions.explanation: It is a short-run law (one factor fixed).

questions.q: In Stage I (increasing returns), marginal product:
questions.explanation: MP rises in Stage I.

questions.q: In Stage III, total product:
questions.explanation: In Stage III, MP is negative and TP falls.

questions.q: A farmer keeps adding workers to a fixed field. Output rises fast at first, then slowly, then falls. This pattern is the:
questions.explanation: Rising-then-falling marginal product with a fixed factor is the law of variable proportions.

questions.q: Diminishing returns set in mainly because, in the short run, the fixed factor:
options: Cannot be increased, so each extra worker has less of it to use
questions.explanation: A constant fixed factor shared among more variable units lowers each unit's extra output.

questions.q: TP values are 0, 12, 28, 40, 48, 48. The marginal product of the 5th unit is:
questions.explanation: MP₅ = TP₅ − TP₄ = 48 − 40 = 8.

questions.q: From the same data, total product is maximum and MP becomes zero at unit:
questions.explanation: TP stops rising at the 6th unit (48 to 48), where MP = 0.

questions.q: A producer is in Stage III where MP is negative. The sensible action is to:
options: Reduce the variable factor and move back to Stage II
questions.explanation: Since extra workers now cut output, the firm should cut back to the rational Stage II.

questions.q: Average product is rising as long as marginal product is:
questions.explanation: When MP exceeds AP it pulls AP up; AP rises until MP = AP at AP's peak.

questions.q: The production function Q = f(L, K) tells us about the ____ relationship, not about money costs.
questions.explanation: It links physical input quantities to physical output, ignoring prices and costs.

questions.q: A bakery can change its workers daily but can only build a bigger oven over a year. Changing only workers is a ____ decision.
questions.explanation: With the oven (capital) fixed and only labour variable, the firm is operating in the short run.

questions.q: In Stage I, increasing returns occur partly because the fixed factor was:
options: Under-utilised, so extra workers improve efficiency
questions.explanation: Early variable units use the spare capacity of the fixed factor better, raising MP.

questions.q: Why can a firm not raise output forever simply by hiring more workers on a fixed plant?
options: Marginal product eventually falls and turns negative
questions.explanation: Diminishing then negative returns mean each extra worker eventually adds less, then reduces, output.
